title: Kerala Built Its Miracle on Gulf Money. Now the Gulf Is Drying Up — and Nobody Has a Plan B.
excerpt: With remittances funding 17% of state GDP and the Hormuz crisis throttling Gulf economies, Kerala’s three-decade economic model is facing an existential test. Morgan Stanley is already warning Delhi.
body:
The numbers are brutal in their simplicity.

In fiscal year 2023–24, Kerala received an estimated $23.4 billion in remittances from its overseas workers — roughly 17.1% of the state’s entire GDP. Maharashtra, India’s largest recipient state in absolute terms, sees remittances at 5% of GDP. Kerala’s reliance is more than triple that. And approximately 80% of Kerala’s overseas workers are based in a single geographic zone: the Persian Gulf.

Now, with the Strait of Hormuz blockade reshaping energy markets, Gulf economies slowing, and construction and hospitality sectors shedding jobs, the money pipeline that built modern Kerala is under threat — and the state has no obvious fallback.

## The Architecture of Dependency

Kerala’s Gulf story is one of the most remarkable migration economies in the developing world. Beginning in the 1970s oil boom, millions of Malayalis — mostly young men from working-class and lower-middle-class families — took construction, hospitality, retail, and domestic service jobs across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, and Bahrain. The remittances they sent home funded houses, education, healthcare, and an entire consumer economy that lifted Kerala’s human development indicators to levels that bewildered economists accustomed to correlating prosperity with industrialisation.

By 2020, an estimated 3.5 million Keralites lived in the Gulf. The Kerala Gulf diaspora is so large that 80% of all Indians in Kuwait are Malayali. The money flowed in two directions: remittances home, and a parallel economy of gold, consumer electronics, and property investment that became the backbone of the state’s middle class.

But the model always had a structural flaw: it was built on a commodity cycle Kerala didn’t control.

## The Hormuz Effect

The immediate trigger is geopolitical. The US-led Strait of Hormuz blockade, imposed in response to Iranian provocations, has sent global oil prices past $100 a barrel and disrupted shipping routes that carry a quarter of the world’s oil and a third of its natural gas. For Gulf economies — which were already diversifying away from oil but remain deeply tied to energy revenue — the blockade has dampened business confidence, slowed construction activity, and triggered job cuts in precisely the sectors where Indian blue-collar workers are concentrated.

Morgan Stanley flagged the risk in a May report: India received $138 billion in remittances in FY2025, up 15% from the previous year. But the composition is shifting. The Gulf’s share has declined from 47% in 2016–17 to 38% in 2023–24, while advanced economies like the US and UK now account for 42%. The bank warned that “policymakers may consider measures to support returning workers as they reintegrate into the domestic economy.”

For Kerala specifically, the warning is existential. A prolonged slowdown in Gulf employment wouldn’t just reduce remittance flows — it would trigger a reverse migration of workers returning to a state with limited industrial capacity and chronic unemployment, particularly among educated youth.

## The Anxiety Surge

Here is the paradox: remittances from West Asia actually spiked in recent weeks. But the surge is driven by fear, not prosperity. Expatriate workers, uncertain about job security and concerned about potential evacuation scenarios, have been accelerating transfers home — essentially front-loading money they might not be able to send later. India has already evacuated 2,549 citizens from Iran and repatriated 3,000 seafarers as the crisis deepened.

This “anxiety remittance” pattern offers a short-term cushion but masks the underlying risk. If the crisis persists, the spike will be followed by a sustained decline as workers lose jobs or are forced to accept lower wages. The ILO has estimated that real labour incomes could decline by as much as $3 trillion globally by 2027, with Asia-Pacific and Arab states among the most exposed regions.

## The Diaspora Angle NRIs Can’t Ignore

For the Indian diaspora in the West — the software engineers in San Jose, the doctors in London, the accountants in Toronto — Kerala’s Gulf dependency might feel like a distant problem. It is not.

Remittances remain the single largest source of foreign exchange for India, financing 40–45% of the merchandise trade deficit. A hit to Gulf remittances weakens the rupee, widens the current account deficit, and creates inflationary pressure that touches every Indian household — including those of NRIs with family, property, or investments in India.

Meanwhile, the same global forces are reshaping migration patterns for the professional diaspora. Visa crackdowns in Canada, the UK, and Australia — which have already threatened 30,000 Kerala students with potential return — mean that the “advanced economy” remittance channel that Morgan Stanley flagged as more stable is itself under pressure.

## What Comes Next

Kerala’s election in April 2026 was fought partly on these anxieties, with Gulf returnees — who now vote in significant numbers — demanding more support for reintegration. But the structural challenge goes beyond any single election cycle.

The state needs industrial jobs that don’t exist, re-skilling programmes that are barely funded, and an economic diversification strategy that successive governments have promised and none have delivered. The remittance model worked spectacularly for three decades. Whether it survives the next three years is an open question.

For NRIs sending money home to Kerala — or watching parents and siblings navigate an economy built on assumptions that are crumbling in real time — the stakes are not abstract. They are personal, immediate, and growing by the day.
